The most common malignancies include non-melanoma skin cancers and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD).51,52 While not all malignancies are a consequence of transplan- tation or immunosuppressive therapy,51 both the duration and intensity of immunosuppression have been linked to this increased incidence.52 Other risk factors include in- creasing age, male gender,53 sun exposure, and cigarette smoking.51 It is difficult to assess the impact of individual drugs on cancer risk;51 some studies have found an increased inci- dence in patients given ciclosporin (compared with azathi- oprine) or muromonab-CD3.53 Data are conflicting on the carcinogenic effects of mycophenolate.51 Proliferation sig- nal inhibitors such as sirolimus and everolimus have been reported to carry less of a risk, possibly as a result of their mode of action.51-54 Although long-term data are needed, some have suggested that conversion from calcineurin in- hibitors to proliferation signal inhibitors should be consid- ered in high-risk patients.52-54 Nonmyeloablative conditioning regimens allowing for the development of immunological tolerance specific to the donor remain the ultimate goal of renal transplantation.4,55 There are reports of the development of chimerism and tol- erance allowing withdrawal of all immunosuppression in a few patients in whom kidney transplants were combined with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.56,57 1.
